title: Why Students Ignore Your Directions
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin diagnoses the common frustration of students ignoring, half-following, or failing to follow directions as a fixable problem rooted in how directions are delivered, not in student capability. He offers a five-step method: be extraordinarily clear so no doubt remains about expectations before allowing action; avoid wordiness and hesitation, modeling step by step instead of merely explaining; use 'going-to' language so students can visualize themselves successfully performing the direction; shift the onus onto students by asking if anyone doesn't understand, which pressures them to listen more closely; and end with a paused 'Go' signal that builds anticipation and prompts a final mental review. His underlying argument is that consistency across every single instance is what turns compliance into an automatic habit, and any inconsistency reintroduces the sloppiness and confusion the method is meant to eliminate.
points: Directions should use 'going-to' language (e.g. 'You're going to take out your laptops...') so students visualize the steps before acting.
Asking who doesn't understand shifts the burden onto students to speak up, which increases listening and accountability.
A deliberate pause before saying 'Go' builds anticipation and prompts one last mental review of the expected steps.
The five-step process must be used every single time to become automatic; inconsistency lets sloppiness and confusion creep back in.
quotes: It’s among the most frustrating classroom management problems. You give directions and your students either ignore them or they . . . kinda-sorta follow them.
In most classrooms students are confused. They halfway listen. They’re partially informed. They’re only nominally aware of what is expected of them.
Wordiness, fluff, and thinking aloud are your enemies. Wait until you know what you want and what it looks like before uttering a word.
Your students must see themselves in their mind's eye successfully performing the directions you give them. This is why modeling is so effective.
Saying “Go” is the most effective way to get students moving. It shakes them from their stillness and launches their purpose, which is to complete your directions.
To make following directions a habit, you must use each of the steps above every time. Otherwise, sloppiness, confusion, and resistance will return.
